title: Cloud Computing (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS)
subtitle: AXIS deep-dive: NIST traits, service & deployment models, providers, cloud vs data centre, virtualization

readingSections.title: What Is Cloud Computing?
readingSections.quickSummary: Renting computing over the Internet on a pay-per-use basis: five NIST traits, provider-run hardware, instant scalability.
content: Cloud computing delivers computing services - servers, storage, databases, networking, software - over the Internet ('the cloud') on a pay-as-per-use model. Instead of buying and housing physical hardware in an on-premises data centre, organisations rent remote hardware from a provider.

NIST defines five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service (provision without human interaction), broad network access (reach from standard devices), resource pooling (multi-tenant hardware sharing), rapid elasticity (scale up/down instantly), and measured service (metered, pay-per-use billing).
The economics: capital expenditure (CAPEX - buying servers) shifts to operational expenditure (OPEX - paying for what you use). This single shift explains most cloud-vs-data-centre PYQ contrasts.

subsections.title: The published PYQ contrast
subsections.content:
On-premises hardware -> DATA CENTRE. Remote hardware rented over the Internet -> CLOUD.
Instant scalability -> cloud. Scalability challenges and delays -> data centre.
Downtime and repairs: OWNER in a data centre, PROVIDER in the cloud.
Pay as per use -> cloud.

subsections.title: Why organisations move to cloud
subsections.content: No upfront hardware cost; global reach in minutes; elasticity absorbs traffic spikes; provider-managed maintenance, security patches and redundancy; measured billing ties cost to usage. Trade-offs: ongoing subscription cost, connectivity dependence, and data-governance questions.

quickRevision: Five traits: on-demand, broad access, pooled, elastic, measured.
CAPEX (buy) becomes OPEX (rent) in the cloud.
Provider fixes cloud hardware; owner fixes data-centre hardware.
Pay-per-use + instant scale = cloud, never data centre.
tricks: Any option pairing 'instant scalable' with 'data centre' is wrong - the published PYQ maps it to cloud.
Statement-pair questions: assign 'owner repairs' to the data centre side and everything else falls into place.
'Remote hardware' in the stem = cloud; 'on-premises' = data centre - verbatim PYQ mapping.
patterns: 'Which is true about cloud and data centre?' - downtime responsibility belongs to the data-centre OWNER.
'Pay as per use' - cloud billing, metered service.

pyqPatterns.question: Which statement is true about cloud and data centre (downtime)?
pyqPatterns.approach: Only 'in data centre, the owner is responsible for downtime and repairs' is true - in cloud the provider handles it.

pyqPatterns.question: Correctly mapped attributes of cloud vs data centre?
pyqPatterns.approach: On-premises -> data centre; remote hardware -> cloud. Instant scalability belongs with cloud.

readingSections.companyNote: Cloud-vs-data-centre contrasts appear in every published AXIS PYQ batch - usually as a statement-pair question.

readingSections.title: Service Models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
readingSections.quickSummary: IaaS = rent infrastructure (you manage OS up); PaaS = rent platform (you bring code); SaaS = rent software (you just use it).
content: Cloud services stack in three layers. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) rents raw compute, storage and network - you install the OS, runtimes and applications (AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine).

PaaS (Platform as a Service) adds the OS, runtime and middleware - you deploy only your code and data (Azure App Service, Heroku, Google App Engine). SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers the finished application through a browser - the provider manages everything (Microsoft 365, Gmail, Salesforce, Dropbox).
The responsibility ladder: On-premises (customer manages EVERYTHING) > IaaS > PaaS > SaaS (customer manages almost nothing). Every PYQ on this topic tests one rung of that ladder.

subsections.title: Recognition phrases
subsections.content:
'Rent virtual machines and install your own OS' -> IaaS.
'Deploy code without managing servers or OS' -> PaaS.
'Use the software in a browser, nothing to install' -> SaaS.

subsections.title: Everyday examples
subsections.content:
IaaS: EC2 instances, Azure VMs, GCE.
PaaS: Azure App Service, Google App Engine, Heroku.
SaaS: Gmail, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Zoom, Dropbox.

quickRevision: I install (IaaS), P just program (PaaS), S just sit-and-use (SaaS).
Responsibility shrinks upward: on-prem > IaaS > PaaS > SaaS.
EC2/Azure VMs = IaaS; App Service/Heroku = PaaS; M365/Gmail = SaaS.
tricks: Match the question's 'you manage...' phrase: OS -> IaaS; only code -> PaaS; nothing -> SaaS.
SaaS distractors often claim the customer patches the OS - in SaaS even the app is provider-managed.
patterns: 'Which model gives VMs where you install the OS?' - IaaS.
'Which model would a developer choose to deploy without managing servers?' - PaaS.

pyqPatterns.question: Map the customer-managed stack from most to least responsibility.
pyqPatterns.approach: On-premises > IaaS > PaaS > SaaS - monotonic ladder.

readingSections.companyNote: One service-model question appears in nearly every AXIS networking/security/cloud slot.

readingSections.title: Deployment Models: Public, Private, Hybrid, Community
readingSections.quickSummary: Public = shared provider infra; Private = one organisation; Hybrid = both orchestrated; Community = shared by similar organisations.
content: Public cloud runs on provider-owned infrastructure shared by many customers (multi-tenant) - AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud. Cheapest, most elastic, least control.

Private cloud dedicates infrastructure to ONE organisation - hosted on-premises or by a third party - for maximum control and compliance. Hybrid cloud combines public and private with orchestration, letting data and apps move between them (sensitive workloads private, bursty workloads public).
Community cloud shares infrastructure among organisations with common concerns (regulation, security posture) - e.g., government clouds.

subsections.title: Selection logic
subsections.content:
Cost-first, general workloads -> public.
Strict compliance/data sovereignty -> private.
Sensitive core + elastic web tier -> hybrid.
Regulated sector peers sharing a platform -> community.

quickRevision: Public = shared, cheap, elastic. Private = dedicated, controlled.
Hybrid = best of both, orchestrated. Community = shared by peers with common rules.
tricks: 'Government agencies sharing one platform' -> community, not private.
'Burst to public for peak load while keeping data private' -> hybrid.

pyqPatterns.question: Which deployment model combines public and private clouds?
pyqPatterns.approach: Hybrid - orchestrated movement between the two.

readingSections.companyNote: Deployment-model identification is a one-mark freebie if the four definitions are memorised.

readingSections.title: Major Providers & Their PYQ Facts
readingSections.quickSummary: AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle, IBM. Published PYQ facts: Azure spans Linux/Windows Server/SQL Server with enterprise security; GCP is the no-backup-support pick in the published set.
content: The big three: Amazon Web Services (AWS) - the market leader with the deepest service catalogue; Microsoft Azure - strongest enterprise/hybrid integration, natively spanning Linux, Windows Server and SQL Server workloads with enhanced security (a published PYQ answer); Google Cloud Platform (GCP) - data analytics and ML strengths.

Others in PYQ options: Oracle Cloud (database-centric), IBM Cloud (enterprise/legacy), Alibaba Cloud (Asia-Pacific). Provider-trivia questions come straight from published sets - memorise the mappings rather than re-deriving them.

Caution: a few published provider-trivia answers (e.g., backup-support or hybrid-storage claims per provider) reflect dated marketing comparisons. Learn them as PYQ facts, but don't treat them as permanent truths.

subsections.title: The PYQ mappings
subsections.content:
Linux + Windows Server + SQL Server + enhanced security -> AZURE (published PYQ).
No backup support wanted (published set) -> Google Cloud.
Binary large objects (BLOB) emphasis (published set) -> Azure.
Hybrid storage absence (published set) -> Google Cloud Platform.
Market leader by catalogue and share -> AWS.

quickRevision: Azure = Linux + Windows + SQL Server enterprise story.
tricks: Provider questions in AXIS come from a small published pool - memorise the five mappings above rather than reasoning.
If the stem lists Microsoft products (Windows Server, SQL Server), the answer is Azure by elimination.
patterns: 'Support for Linux, Windows Server and SQL Server with enhanced security' -> Azure.
'Choose a provider WITHOUT backup support' -> Google Cloud (published set).

pyqPatterns.question: Which provider for Linux, Windows Server and SQL Server support with enhanced security?
Which provider if you do NOT want backup support?
pyqPatterns.approach: Google Cloud - published answer (dated trivia, learn as PYQ fact).

readingSections.companyNote: Provider-trivia is pure recall from published sets - five facts cover every instance seen publicly.

readingSections.title: Virtualization, Containers & the Data Centre Contrast
readingSections.quickSummary: Virtualization splits one machine into many VMs via a hypervisor; containers share the host OS. Data centre = owner-run hardware; cloud = provider-run.
content: Virtualization is the technology under ALL cloud computing: a hypervisor (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) slices one physical machine into multiple virtual machines, each with its own OS. Resource pooling and multi-tenancy are hypervisor tricks at heart.

Containers (Docker, Kubernetes) go lighter: they share the HOST operating system kernel, packaging only the app and its dependencies - start in milliseconds versus minutes for VMs. VMs isolate more; containers are denser and faster.

The data-centre contrast completes the picture: on-premises means YOU buy, house, power, cool, patch and repair the hardware - the owner owns every failure. In the cloud the provider carries that burden while you consume metered service.

subsections.title: VM vs container
subsections.content:
VM: hypervisor + full guest OS per VM - heavy, minutes to boot, strong isolation.
Container: shares host kernel - lightweight, seconds/milliseconds, denser packing.
Orchestration: Kubernetes schedules and scales containers across hosts.

subsections.title: Type-1 vs Type-2 hypervisors
subsections.content:
Type-1 (bare-metal) runs directly on hardware - ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM - data-centre grade.
Type-2 runs ON a host OS - VirtualBox, VMware Workstation - desktop grade.

quickRevision: Hypervisor slices hardware into VMs; Type-1 bare-metal, Type-2 desktop.
Containers share the host OS - faster, denser; Kubernetes orchestrates.
Data centre: owner's hardware, owner's repairs. Cloud: provider's hardware, provider's repairs.
tricks: 'Shares the host kernel' in the stem -> container, not VM.
Downtime-responsibility statement pairs: owner -> data centre, provider -> cloud.
patterns: 'Lightweight, shares host OS, starts in seconds' - containers.
'Multi-tenant resource pooling' - virtualization enabling public cloud.

pyqPatterns.question: Cloud vs data centre responsibility statements.
pyqPatterns.approach: Owner repairs = data centre only; provider repairs = cloud only.

readingSections.companyNote: Virtualization questions appear in the broader AXIS pool (and in interviews) - VM/container distinction is the one to know cold.

formulas.title: NIST Five Essential Characteristics

formula.text: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.

formulas.whenToUse: 'Which are the essential characteristics of cloud computing?' questions.
explanation: On-demand: provision without human negotiation.
Broad access: any standard device over the network.
Pooling: multi-tenant hardware abstraction.
Elasticity: scale out/in on demand.
Measured: usage is metered and billed.

formula.text: Customer-managed stack shrinks as the model rises.

formulas.whenToUse: Mapping 'you manage...' statements to service models.
explanation: On-prem: customer manages everything including hardware.
IaaS: customer manages OS and above (EC2, Azure VMs).
PaaS: customer manages code and data only (App Service, Heroku).
SaaS: customer just uses the app (M365, Gmail).

explanation: Public: multi-tenant, cheapest, most elastic.
Private: dedicated, maximum control/compliance.

formulas.title: Cloud vs Data Centre Contrast Table

formula.text: On-premises/owner-run = data centre; remote rented hardware = cloud; instant scale and pay-per-use = cloud.

explanation: Hardware ownership: DC = you; cloud = provider.
Downtime/repairs: DC = owner; cloud = provider.
Scalability: instant (cloud) vs challenging/delayed (DC).
Billing: pay-per-use metered (cloud) vs capital purchase (DC).

steps: Assign owner-repairs to the DC side.
Only 'data centre owner is responsible' is true.

formulas.title: CAPEX to OPEX Shift

formula.text: Cloud converts upfront capital expenditure into metered operational expenditure.

formulas.whenToUse: 'Why do organisations adopt cloud?' economics questions.
explanation: Buying servers = CAPEX with depreciation and over-provisioning.
Cloud = OPEX: pay for consumed capacity, scale to zero in quiet periods.
Elasticity removes capacity-guessing; measured service ties cost to usage.

example.prompt: Which cost model does cloud introduce?

formulas.commonMistake: Claiming cloud eliminates ALL IT cost - it shifts and meters it.

mcqs.q: Cloud computing delivers computing services:
opts: Over the Internet on a pay-as-per-use basis
exp: Definition: remote, metered services over the Internet.
Pay-per-use replaces upfront hardware purchase.

exp: Five NIST traits include rapid elasticity - scale out/in on demand.
Provisioning is SELF-service, not manual.

mcqs.q: 'Pay as per use' billing belongs to:
exp: Measured, metered billing = cloud economics.

mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Owner-run hardware means owner-run repairs - the published PYQ fact.

mcqs.q: Who handles hardware repairs in the CLOUD?
exp: The provider owns and operates cloud hardware.
Customers consume; they never rack and repair.

mcqs.q: 'On-premises: data centre; remote hardware: cloud' is:
